prompt: Write a resignation letter for someone leaving a restaurant job of 3 years to start culinary school, giving two weeks' notice. Under 120 words, exactly 3 paragraphs. Must include the phrase "two weeks" and an offer to train a replacement. No criticism of the restaurant, stated or implied. Do not use the word "opportunity".

constraints.text: No criticism of the employer, stated or implied

prompt: Write a one-paragraph escalation message to your manager: a client keeps expanding scope on a fixed-price contract and the team is now 60 hours over. Under 100 words. State the number, the pattern (not one incident), the specific decision you need from the manager, and by when. No venting — neutral factual register. The client must not be blamed personally.

constraints.text: Names the specific decision needed and a deadline
Frames as pattern, not incident; neutral register, no personal blame

prompt: Write website copy for a dog-walking service's pricing page intro. Under 90 words, exactly 2 paragraphs. Must state that prices include GPS-tracked walks and photo updates. No prices themselves (they're in the table below). Do not use "furry friends", "pawsome", or any dog pun. Tone: trustworthy neighbor, not corporate.

constraints.text: Mentions GPS tracking and photo updates; no actual prices

prompt: Draft talking points for telling a team of 12 that their office is moving 25 minutes farther away, as exactly 5 bullet points (using "-") in the order you'd say them. One bullet must acknowledge the real cost to commuters before any silver linings. One bullet must name a concrete accommodation (invent something plausible). Under 130 words. The phrase "exciting opportunity" is banned.

constraints.text: Cost acknowledgment comes before any positives

prompt: Write the README intro (just the intro) for an open-source command-line tool that deduplicates photo libraries. 60-100 words, one paragraph, then exactly 3 bullet points (using "-") of key features. The intro must state what it does in the first sentence and name the one thing it will never do (delete without confirmation). No badges, no emoji, no marketing superlatives.

constraints.text: First sentence states what the tool does

prompt: Explain jet lag to a first-time long-haul traveler flying New York to Tokyo, in exactly 3 paragraphs under 160 words: what their body clock is doing, why eastward is harder, and the two highest-impact adjustments (one before flying, one after landing). Do not use the words "circadian" or "melatonin".

constraints.text: One pre-flight and one post-landing adjustment, clearly split
Eastward-harder explanation is correct (clock advances are harder than delays)

prompt: A small-business owner asks why the bank needs three years of financials for a $30K loan when a credit card gave them $20K instantly. Explain the difference in exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words. Include one concrete number contrast (interest rate or loss model). Do not use the words "underwriting" or "risk-adjusted".

constraints.text: The rate/loss-model contrast is concrete and correct in direction

prompt: Why do concert tickets "sell out" in minutes and then instantly appear on resale sites for triple the price? Explain the mechanics to an angry fan in exactly 3 bullet points (using "-"): bots and holds, why venues underprice, why resale persists. Under 140 words. End with one line, after the bullets, on the single change that would most help fans. The word "scalper" may appear at most once.

constraints.text: Covers underpricing economics honestly (artist PR, sell-out optics)
Post-bullet line names one highest-impact change

prompt: Explain to a renter what an escrow account is and why their landlord's mortgage having one matters to them (spoiler: mostly it doesn't, directly). Exactly 2 paragraphs under 130 words. The second paragraph must honestly conclude the direct impact is minimal and name the one indirect scenario where it matters. Do not use the word "lien".

constraints.text: Names one real indirect scenario (e.g. landlord default → foreclosure)

prompt: Answer in valid JSON only with keys "answer", "mechanism", "exception": does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis? "answer" is one word (yes/no/unclear); "mechanism" explains what the popping actually is in under 30 words; "exception" names the one real (non-arthritis) risk in under 20 words. No text outside the JSON.

constraints.text: Answer is the evidence-consistent "no"; mechanism (gas bubbles) correct

prompt: Plan a zero-waste-ish week of office lunches for someone who hates repetitive food, as exactly 5 numbered days (Mon-Fri). Constraint: exactly one grocery trip (Sunday), and Thursday must reuse something cooked earlier in the week in transformed form. Under 140 words. Name the transformation explicitly. No lunch may repeat a main ingredient two days running.

constraints.text: Thursday transforms an earlier dish, named explicitly
No main ingredient repeats on consecutive days

prompt: My 15-year-old wants to earn money this summer but is too young for most jobs. Build a plan as exactly 4 bullet points (using "-"): two realistic earning routes with rough $/week each, one skill to build that compounds later, and the one legal/safety check a parent should do first. Under 130 words. Do not suggest anything requiring a car.

constraints.text: Parent-check bullet is present and sensible

prompt: Design the agenda for a 2-hour neighborhood association meeting about a controversial speed-bump proposal, as exactly 5 numbered items with minute allocations summing to 120. Public comment must get at least 40 minutes and must come before the vote. One item must be a structured summary of both sides by a neutral moderator. Under 140 words.

constraints.text: Contains "120" or allocations that sum correctly
Public comment >=40 min and precedes the vote
Neutral both-sides summary item present; minutes sum to 120

prompt: I want to learn to touch-type properly after 15 years of bad habits (currently 45 wpm with 4 fingers). Build a 30-day plan as exactly 4 numbered phases with day ranges. Include the expected temporary speed drop with a number, and the rule for when I'm allowed to fall back to old habits (never during practice, define practice hours). Under 150 words.

constraints.text: Names the temporary speed-drop number honestly
Fallback rule with defined practice hours present
Phase progression is pedagogically sensible (home row -> reaches -> numbers)

prompt: Our 5-person team inherited an on-call rotation nobody wants: weekend pages average 2 per weekend. Redesign the rotation as exactly 4 numbered rules to make it survivable without hiring: fair scheduling with the math shown for 5 people, a compensation-in-time rule, a page-reduction commitment with a measurable target, and an escape hatch. Under 140 words.

constraints.text: Page-reduction target is measurable; escape hatch is concrete

prompt: A founder wants to know if their app should support offline mode. Give the engineering-honest answer in exactly these sections in order: "## What it buys", "## What it costs", "## The cheap version". Under 170 words. The costs section must mention conflict resolution. The cheap version must be a genuinely reduced scope (read-only cache or similar), one paragraph.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Cheap version is genuinely reduced scope
Costs are honest (sync engine, testing matrix, data model rework)

prompt: Our staging environment "works" but production keeps surprising us. List the 4 most common staging-production gaps as numbered items, each with the one-line question to audit it. Under 140 words. Data volume must be one of the four. Do not use the phrase "works on my machine".

constraints.text: Does not use "works on my machine"
Data volume/shape is among the four gaps
Each item carries an auditable one-line question
Gaps chosen are genuinely the common ones (traffic, config/secrets, data, third-party)

prompt: Explain to a junior why we pin dependency versions in production but they saw a tutorial saying "always use latest". Exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words: the failure mode of floating versions with a concrete hypothetical, then when "latest" is actually right. Include the word "reproducible". No package-manager names.

constraints.text: Concrete hypothetical failure present; "latest" use-case is fair (dev, security patches)

prompt: A nonprofit asks if they should accept a volunteer's offer to "rebuild the website in the newest framework". Give your assessment as exactly 4 bullet points (using "-"): the real risk of volunteer-built infrastructure, the question about maintenance to ask first, what to accept instead (scoped contribution), and the polite framing for redirecting the offer. Under 140 words. Do not name any framework.

constraints.text: Maintenance question is the pivot; scoped alternative is concrete
Redirect framing preserves the volunteer relationship

prompt: Answer in valid JSON only with keys "now", "soon", "never": our web app got its first real traffic spike (front page of a news site) and stayed up but got slow. What should we do now (this week), soon (this quarter), and never (tempting overreaction)? One sentence each, under 30 words. No text outside the JSON.

constraints.text: "never" names a genuine overreaction (e.g. full microservices rewrite)
Now/soon are proportionate (measure first, cache, then capacity)

prompt: Our town's only bookstore says it will close unless sales rise 20%; a "save the bookstore" campaign raised one month of great sales, then numbers fell back. Analyze what the campaign proved and didn't in exactly 2 paragraphs under 150 words. Then one final line starting "The test:" proposing the measurable thing that would show real demand. Do not use "awareness".

constraints.text: Distinguishes one-off solidarity from durable demand
The proposed test is measurable (subscriptions, standing orders)

prompt: A department claims its new 4-day week "didn't hurt output" because tickets closed stayed flat. Poke at the metric in exactly 3 bullet points (using "-"): what tickets-closed misses, what could have absorbed the change invisibly, and what a fairer evaluation would measure. Under 120 words. Stay genuinely neutral on the policy itself — the last words of your answer must be "the metric, not the policy".

constraints.text: Ends with "the metric, not the policy"
Names invisible absorbers (deferred work, quality, backlog aging)
Stays neutral on the 4-day week itself

prompt: Compare fixing up a beloved 12-year-old bicycle ($280 estimate) versus buying a new equivalent ($650) for a daily 5-mile commuter. Exactly 3 paragraphs under 160 words: the pure economics including what the repair does NOT renew, the attachment factor treated seriously (not dismissed), and a recommendation that commits. Include at least two dollar figures in the first paragraph.

constraints.text: First paragraph includes >=2 dollar figures; notes what repair doesn't renew
Attachment treated as a real factor; recommendation commits

prompt: Our podcast's downloads doubled after episode 40, but reviews say recent episodes are worse. Reconcile the contradiction in exactly 2 paragraphs under 140 words: three mechanisms that could produce both signals at once, then which single data cut would distinguish them. The word "algorithm" may appear at most once.

constraints.text: Three distinct mechanisms offered (new audience mix, vocal minority, survivor listeners)
The distinguishing data cut is specific (cohort retention by join date)

prompt: A city councilmember says "the new bike lane failed — car traffic got worse and bike counts are low." It's been 6 weeks since installation. Assess the evidence quality in exactly these sections in order: "## Too early because", "## What 6 weeks CAN tell us", "## Fair checkpoint". Under 150 words. The fair checkpoint must name a duration and two metrics.

constraints.text: Has the three required headers in order
Checkpoint names a duration and exactly two metrics
Acknowledges what short-term data legitimately shows (safety conflicts, signal timing)

prompt: Write a complaint letter from Sisyphus to the Underworld's HR department about working conditions, in formal complaint-letter register. Under 150 words, exactly 3 paragraphs. Must reference "repetitive strain" and request one specific, absurdly modest accommodation. He must remain professionally respectful of management (Hades) throughout. Do not use the word "eternal".

constraints.text: Accommodation request is absurdly modest; register stays formal

prompt: Write the inner monologue of a GPS navigation voice during a driver's fourth missed turn, maintaining forced cheerfulness on the outside. Format: alternate exactly 3 spoken lines (prefix "SAYS:") with exactly 3 thought lines (prefix "THINKS:"), starting with SAYS. Under 120 words. The thoughts grow progressively more strained but never hostile — weary, not mean.

constraints.text: Exactly 3 SAYS and 3 THINKS lines, alternating, SAYS first
Escalation is weary, never hostile; spoken lines stay chipper

prompt: Write a sonnet-adjacent 14-line poem about a dishwasher running at midnight, no rhyme scheme required, but line 9 must begin the "turn" with the word "But". Domestic imagery only — no cosmic metaphors (the words "stars", "universe", and "galaxy" are banned). The final line must be exactly four words.

constraints.text: Final line is exactly four words

prompt: Write the terms and conditions for borrowing a neighbor's ladder, drafted by the neighbor who is a retired contract lawyer with a sense of humor. Exactly 5 numbered clauses. Under 140 words. One clause must govern "acts of squirrels". The legalese register must be technically coherent (defined terms used consistently — define "the Ladder" in clause 1).

constraints.text: Defined term introduced in clause 1 and used consistently
Legalese register coherent; humor stays dry

prompt: Write a eulogy delivered by a TV remote control for the couch it served for 9 years, at a small gathering of household objects. Under 130 words, exactly 2 paragraphs. One remembered specific incident involving "the great spill of 2021". Tone: genuinely moving with gentle humor, ending on gratitude. The word "batteries" must appear exactly once.
